processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: 50 kg ingots of the 1.2C steel prepared by induction melting under an argon atmosphere.
Homogenized at the same temperature (1200 °C) for 3 h prior to hot rolling.
Hot rolled to a thickness of 3.5 mm with a reduction of 90%.
Hot-rolled strips annealed at 1000 °C for 1 h before cold rolling.
Cold rolled to a thickness of 1 mm.
Cold rolled strips annealed at 1000 °C (final annealing giving the as-quenched state).
Followed by water quenching to room temperature, giving the as-quenched terminal state.

structures.overall_structure: Fully austenitic (γ) matrix microstructure with some annealing twins in grains and κ carbides uniformly distributed in the austenite matrix.

phases_present.morphology: coarse equiaxed polygonal grains with straight, parallel-sided annealing twins
fine, uniformly distributed precipitates (fine bright speckle in dark-field TEM)

precipitates.distribution: uniformly distributed in the austenite matrix

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Tensile tests carried out at room temperature on a universal testing machine (SANSCMT5000) at constant crosshead displacement velocity (equivalent to an initial strain rate of 1.33×10^-3 s^-1).

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress–strain curve of 1.2C steel in Fig. 3 (green curve), plateau near 940 MPa, extending to roughly 0.55–0.6 strain.

strain_hardening_rate.value: three-stage strain hardening; steep first stage, flat plateau at roughly ln(dσ/dε) ≈ 7.5, then a rising third stage; after 0.026 strain the 1.2C steel sustains a sufficient strain hardening rate

comparative_performance.improvement_percentage: UTS × TE reaches 53205 MPa·%, almost twice as high as that of the 0.5C steel

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: specimens prepared by standard mechanical polishing and etching with a solution of 1 ml hydrochloric acid, 100 ml methanol and 4 g picric acid
characterization_methods.purpose: observe representative optical microstructure of the as-quenched 1.2C steel
characterization_methods.key_findings: 1.2C steel is fully austenitic with coarse equiaxed polygonal grains and abundant straight, parallel-sided annealing twins (Fig. 1(c)).

characterization_methods.technique: transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with selected-area diffraction (SADP)
characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Tecnai G2 20 TEM at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV; thin foils prepared by twinjet electropolishing in 9% perchloric acid in methanol at −30 °C
characterization_methods.purpose: identify phases and precipitates in the austenite matrix
characterization_methods.key_findings: 1.2C steel contains some κ carbides in the matrix of austenite (Fig. 2(f)); dark-field image of γ phase shows fine bright speckle throughout; SADP indexed 131, 220, 110, 111.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: room temperature, constant crosshead displacement velocity equivalent to an initial strain rate of 1.33×10^-3 s^-1
characterization_methods.purpose: determine mechanical properties of the as-quenched 1.2C steel

characterization_methods.technique: Crussard–Jaoul (C–J) analysis of strain hardening (ln(dσ/dε) vs ln ε)
characterization_methods.purpose: analyze strain hardening stages of the 1.2C steel
characterization_methods.key_findings: 1.2C steel exhibits a three-stage strain hardening with breakpoints at ε=0.026 and ε=0.137 (Fig. 5(c)).

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: interrupted tensile tests at true strains 0.02, 0.07, 0.3 and 0.4
characterization_methods.purpose: track microstructural evolution (dislocation substructure) of the 1.2C steel during plastic deformation
characterization_methods.key_findings: Planar slip at ε 0.02, Taylor lattice-like structure at ε 0.07, well-developed microbands at ε 0.3, and interaction between microbands at ε 0.4 (Fig. 8).

computational_details.potential_model_or_database: density calculation [Ref. 7]; stacking fault energy model used previously [Ref. 13]

analytical_models.equation_role: predict density of the steel from composition

analytical_models.model_note: SFE value of austenite in 1.2C steel = 84.5 mJ/m2 (0.5C and 0.8C steels are 73.4 and 77.9 mJ/m2).

unmapped_findings: The austenite stacking fault energy (SFE) of the 1.2C steel is 84.5 mJ/m2, calculated according to the model used previously [13] (b0016).
The density of the 1.2C steel was calculated [7] as 6.78 g/cm3 (b0016).
The UTS × TE value of the 1.2C steel reaches 53205 MPa·%, almost twice as high as that of the 0.5C steel (28100 MPa·%) (figure_004, b0037, b0024).
Three-stage strain hardening of the 1.2C steel described by C–J analysis has breakpoints at ε = 0.026 and ε = 0.137 (figure_005, b0051).

Microstructural evolution of the 1.2C steel during tensile deformation: planar slip (ε 0.02) → Taylor lattice (ε 0.07) → well-developed microbands (ε 0.3) → interaction of microbands (ε 0.4) (figure_008, b0029, b0060).

The fast decline of strain hardening in the first stage of the 1.2C steel is mainly related to the easiness of planar slip in the austenite matrix; the second stage is associated with formation of Taylor lattice and microbands; the last stage is explained by increased microband density and microband interaction (b0054).
